concepts.offTopic: Light passes through a normal 1 m wide doorway. Does it diffract, or does diffraction only happen at narrow slits?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think you need a really small opening for diffraction to happen
concepts.misconceptionSource: seed probe misconception-tagged choice (verbatim, first-personed)
concepts.correctTyped: It DIFFRACTS — diffraction is universal for all apertures. What decides whether you SEE the pattern is the ratio a/λ. For a 1 m door and visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm), a/λ ≈ 2×10⁶, and the central diffraction maximum spreads through only about 0.5 μrad — utterly invisible, but there. Narrow the opening down until a ≈ λ (a slit ~1 μm wide) and the pattern becomes observable; walk through an audio-wavelength doorway (λ ≈ 1 m) and you hear diffraction easily — same physics, different a/λ
concepts.wrongTyped: No — you need a really small opening for diffraction to happen

concepts.offTopic: In a single-slit diffraction pattern, are all the secondary maxima the same brightness as each other, the way Young's double-slit fringes are?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think they should all be the same brightness, like Young's fringes
concepts.misconceptionSource: seed probe misconception-tagged choice (verbatim, first-personed)
concepts.correctTyped: No — the secondary maxima DECAY under a sinc² envelope. The first sits near α ≈ 3π/2 with I/I₀ ≈ 4/(9π²) ≈ 0.045 — about 22× dimmer than the central peak; the second near α ≈ 5π/2 with I/I₀ ≈ 4/(25π²) ≈ 0.016, about 61× dimmer. Young's equal-intensity fringes come from two POINT sources contributing equal amplitude at every angle; single-slit intensity is the FT of a uniform aperture, and the phasor sum shrinks with angle, so the envelope monotonically decays
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — they should all be the same brightness, like Young's fringes
